lesson.title: The Price of Removing an Electron
lesson.summary: Ionization energy is the energy needed to pull an electron away from a gaseous atom, and its rise and fall across the periodic table maps directly onto how tightly the nucleus grips its electrons.
lesson.body:
Every atom holds its electrons through the electrical attraction between the positively charged nucleus and the negatively charged electron cloud. Ionization energy measures how strong that grip is: it is the minimum energy required to remove one electron from a neutral atom in the gas phase, written as X(g) plus energy yields X+(g) plus an electron. Because you are always fighting an attractive force to pull the electron free, this process is endothermic, so first ionization energy values are always positive, typically reported in kilojoules per mole. A small ionization energy means the outer electron is loosely held, while a large one means the atom clings to its electrons tightly.

The periodic trend for ionization energy follows directly from effective nuclear charge and atomic radius, which is why it is usually taught alongside periodic trends and valence electron count. Moving left to right across a period, protons are added to the nucleus one at a time while electrons fill the same outer shell, so shielding barely changes but nuclear charge climbs. The valence electrons feel a steadily stronger pull and sit closer to the nucleus, so more energy is needed to remove one. Lithium, at the far left of period 2, has a first ionization energy of only 520 kilojoules per mole, while fluorine, five columns to the right, requires 1681 kilojoules per mole to lose an electron. The same climb shows up in period 3: sodium's lone 3s electron pulls free with just 496 kilojoules per mole, but chlorine holds on until 1251 kilojoules per mole is supplied.

Moving down a group reverses the trend. Each row adds a whole new principal energy level, so the valence electron sits farther from the nucleus and is shielded by an additional layer of core electrons. Even though the nuclear charge is larger, the outer electron feels roughly the same effective pull from a much greater distance, so it is easier to remove. Lithium's first ionization energy of 520 kilojoules per mole drops to 496 for sodium and falls further to 419 for potassium, even though potassium has far more protons than lithium.

Real periodic trends are not perfectly smooth, and the exceptions are worth understanding rather than memorizing away. Beryllium, with its filled 2s2 configuration, has a higher first ionization energy, 899 kilojoules per mole, than boron, 801 kilojoules per mole, even though boron sits one place to the right. A filled s subshell is a stable, low energy arrangement, and boron's extra electron sits in a higher energy 2p orbital that is comparatively easy to remove. A similar dip appears between nitrogen and oxygen: nitrogen's half filled 2p3 configuration is unusually stable, giving it a first ionization energy of 1402 kilojoules per mole, while oxygen's 2p4 configuration forces two electrons into one orbital, and the extra repulsion there makes oxygen's electron easier to remove, at 1314 kilojoules per mole, despite oxygen having one more proton.

Ionization energy predicts how atoms behave chemically. Elements with low ionization energies, like the alkali metals, lose electrons readily and form cations, which is exactly why sodium and potassium are so reactive. Elements with high ionization energies, like the halogens and noble gases, resist losing electrons and instead tend to gain them. This single property sets up two ideas that build directly on it: successive ionization energies, which track what happens when you keep removing electrons past the first, and electronegativity, which measures an atom's pull on electrons it already shares in a bond.
